If everything goes correctly, the service can finally read the information about
the user, including the groups to which they belong, and according to its access
rules, grant or deny them access to the service. If authentication is successful,
the service responds to the client with an AP-REP message by encrypting the
timestamp with the extracted session key. The client can then verify that this
message is coming from the service and can start issuing service requests.

• DC verifies that the service has the right to delegate authentication to the requested resource
• DC verifies that the copy of the TGS ticket or Service Ticket is forwardable (which is the default but can
be disabled if the "Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated" flag is set in the user's UAC flags).
If all goes well, it will return a TGS ticket or Service Ticket to the service with the information of the user
to be delegated to consume the final resource.
Resource-based constrained delegation shifts delegation management to the final resource. It is no longer at the
service level that we list the resources to which we can delegate, but at the resource level, a trust list is
established. Any account on this trusted list has the right to delegate authentication to access the resource.
In this example, the trusted list of the account DBSRV$ contains only the account WEBSRV$. Thus, a
user will be authorized if WEBSRV$ wishes to impersonate a user to access a service exposed by DBSRV.
On the other hand, other accounts are not allowed to delegate authentication to any service provided by

The delegation request is the same as for constrained delegation. A TGS
request is made by the service account to access a specific resource. A copy of
the user's TGS ticket is embedded in this request. The Domain Controller will
then check that this service is indeed in the trusted list of the requested
resource. If this is the case, it will provide the service with a TGS ticket to
access this resource as the user.
An active Directory Extension, corresponds to the TGS request made by a service
account to impersonate a user. The service account makes this TGS request to access
a specific resource, and a copy of the user's TGS ticket is embedded in this request.
The Domain Controller will then check that the service has the right to delegate
authentication to the requested resource. If this is the case, it will provide the service
with a TGS ticket to access this resource as the user.

The S4U2Self extension allows a service to obtain a forwardable TGS
ticket to itself on behalf of an arbitrary user.
When a user authenticates to the service via NTLM for example, the
service will first request a forwardable TGS to itself on behalf of the
user to act as if the user had authenticated via Kerberos, then once
the service has this special TGS ticket, it can make its TGS request to
use the desired resource (S4U2Proxy), embedding the brand new
forwardable TGS ticket it just asked for.
This extension allows delegation even if the authentication
protocol is not always the same between the user and the
different services. This is called protocol transition.
It is precisely this feature that can be

The Golden Ticket attack allows attackers to forge and sign TGTs (Ticket Granting Tickets) using the krbtgt account’s NTLM hash. Since AD servers trust tickets signed with this key, attackers can
create tickets for non-existent users or elevate privileges (e.g., to Domain Admin). They can then request TGS (Ticket Granting Service) tickets to access remote machines.
- Attackers extract the krbtgt hash via DCSync (Mimikatz) or SecretsDump (Impacket).
- Changing the krbtgt password requires two resets and domain-wide replication (~24 hours).
- The PAC (Privilege Attribute Certificate) inside TGTs stores user details and is copied into TGS tickets.
- Attackers with the krbtgt hash can decrypt, modify, and re-encrypt TGTs, granting persistent access.
- The attack is often combined with Pass-the-Ticket, allowing attackers to impersonate privileged users.
- Long-term persistence in an AD environment.
- Potential to evade monitoring by impersonating less-observed privileged accounts.

- Hard to detect: Since Golden Tickets are valid TGTs, Windows event logs don't
- Password reset doesn’t revoke access: Changing the impersonated account’s
password does not invalidate an active Golden Ticket.
- Extended lifespan: Attackers often set long validity periods (e.g., 10 years by
default in Mimikatz), which can be an Indicator of Compromise (IoC).
- The ACCOUNT DOMAIN field is blank.
- The ACCOUNT DOMAIN field contains the FQDN instead of the short domain
- Change the krbtgt password twice to revoke all existing Golden Tickets.
- Regularly rotate the krbtgt password to reduce persistence risks.

Importing and Using the Golden Ticket
Different elements are needed to forge a Golden Ticket:
- Machine Accounts & NTLM Hashes: Each machine has an NTLM hash (SYSTEM$ account), acting as a Pre-Shared Key (PSK)
for signing TGS (Ticket Granting Service) tickets in Kerberos.
- Normally, a user presents a TGT to the DC, which issues a TGS with user info in the PAC (Privilege Attribute Certificate).
- The TGS is encrypted with the service account’s password.
- If an attacker compromises a service/machine account, they can extract its NTLM hash.
- With this, they can forge a TGS by embedding fake user/group info in the PAC.
- The TGS is encrypted with the stolen secret, so the target service accepts it as legitimate.
- Unlike Golden Tickets, Silver Tickets do not interact with the DC, making them harder to detect.
- Logs are only generated on the target machine, reducing visibility in Domain Controller logs.
✅ Monitor event logs on target systems (not just DCs).
✅ Use strong service account passwords & rotate them regularly.
✅ Implement Kerberos authentication protections, like enabling PAC validation.
✅ Detect unusual service ticket activity, such as long lifespans or unexpected user accounts.
• Golden Ticket: Forged TGT, requires interaction with the Domain Controller (DC).
• Silver Ticket: Forged TGS, directly grants access to a target without DC interaction,
Requirements to Forge a Silver Ticket
- NTLM hash of a service/machine account

Silver Tickets are more limited than Golden Tickets, as they target a specific
service on a specific host. However, they offer stealth and can enable long-term
persistence if used to access computer-hosted services, especially when computer
account passwords are not rotated. Detection methods include for when tickets

• The account DOMAIN field contains DOMAIN FQDN instead of just domain.
